MR. HARKNESS  PRESS RELEASE RESPECTING FIRST ALBERTA MEMBER OF PARLIAMENT
speechtext:
I rise on a question of privilege. It has to do with the perpetration of a distortion of history, or an attempt to rewrite part of the early history of the province from which I come, namely Alberta. I have in my hand a press release put out by the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources which states:
Two plaques honouring Frank Oliver, founder and publisher of the Edmonton Bulletin and first member of the House of Commons for Alberta, will be unveiled in a joint ceremony by resources minister Arthur Laing and Edmonton mayor William Hawrelak on Monday, August 17.
Further on the press release states:
Oliver founded the Edmonton Bulletin in 1880 and was publisher of the newspaper until 1923. He was the first elected member for Alberta in the House of Commons-
These statements that Hon. Frank Oliver was the first member of the House of Commons from Alberta are completely incorrect. The Parliamentary Guide, which contains a history of the constituencies of Alberta, states, under the information for my own constituency of Calgary North:
In 1887, when the old Northwest Territories were first given representation in parliament, the whole of the old territory of Alberta was created an electoral division with one member. In 1903, the territory was divided into four constituencies, and by the Act of 1906-07, the representation was increased to seven.
The record of the original district of Alberta was as follows:
1887-W. W. Davis, Conservative
1891-W. W. Davis, Conservative
1896-Frank Oliver, Liberal
1900-Frank Oliver, Liberal
Then it goes on to state:
Under the act of 1902, Alberta was divided into four constituencies, Alberta, Calgary, Strathcona and Edmonton, the electoral records of which, up to 1908, were as follows-
And the members elected in the first election in 1904 were: Alberta, John Herron;
Calgary, M. S. McCarthy; Strathcona, Peter Talbot; and Edmonton, Frank Oliver.
I fail to understand how the department of northern affairs came to put out a press release of this kind. The inaccuracy is repeated in various other ways. For instance, only last night there was an editorial in the Ottawa Journal stating that Frank Oliver was the first elected member from Alberta, and so on.
I have, of course, no desire in the world to take anything away from the position Hon. Frank Oliver holds in the history of Alberta, and I fully agree with this plaque having been put up to his memory. The fault, however, was not that of the historic sites and monuments board. I have received a copy of the inscription on the plaque that was erected, and there is nothing incorrect on it and no statement that he was the first elected member for Alberta.
Under these circumstances, Mr. Speaker, I think the only thing the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources can do is issue another press release correcting the first one and apologizing for it. He should also give due credit to W. W. Davis, who was the first member elected for Alberta. I also suggest that a plaque should be erected to W. W. Davis.

However, I think Alberta entered confederation in 1905, and the statement we made was

When the province was divided into four constituencies and sent four members to parliament at the time of becoming a province, the constituency of Alberta itself was represented by John Herron.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. It has to do with the report that Great Britain has withdrawn 198 troops from its contingent in the United Nations Cyprus force. Was the Canadian government consulted regarding this matter? Is this the first of a series of withdrawals, or is this the only withdrawal which is contemplated by the government of the United Kingdom?

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the 25th of June the secretary of state for commonwealth relations announced that it was the intention of the British government to reduce the size of their contingent in the United Nations force, which at that time numbered 1,800, to between 1,100 and 1,200 men. It is in consequence of that statement that the strength of the British contingent as of the 14th of August was reduced to 1,034.
However, this figure is not to be regarded as completely final because part of the reduction effected consists of troops which are being rotated. There are indications that when this rotation has been completed the figure for the United Kingdom contingent will be increased to the point where the British and Canadian contingents will be roughly equivalent in size. The figure for the Canadian

contingent as of the 14th of August was 1,130. British logistic support, which is of course of vital importance to the whole force, is being maintained at its present level.

subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. Can the minister give the house the assurance that there will be no unilateral withdrawal of Canadian troops until such time as the United Nations itself decides that they can no longer fill a useful role as a peace keeping force in Cyprus?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend will remember that I dealt with this question some time ago, and within the context of what I said then, of course, the decision is one for the United Nations.

subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext: May I ask the minister a further supplementary question with reference to the announcement that an agreement has been reached between the United Nations and Archbishop Makarios regarding the partial lifting of the blockade against the Turkish Cypriots. I would like to ask the minister whether this does not make it clear that the government of Cyprus has been blockading the Turkish Cypriots and seeking to starve them into submission, and whether this does not make it perfectly apparent that Archbishop Makarios, behind the screen of the United Nations peace keeping force, has been systematically seeking to liquidate his opposition?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subsubtopic: CYPRUS-REQUEST FOR STATEMENT ON PRESENT POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend's commentary will speak for itself. There is an agreement now with the government of Cyprus, arranged by the United Nations representatives, to provide for the immediate re-establishment of the water supply in the affected area and to provide for an adequate flow of food and fuel. This arrangement also assumes that the Turkish Cypriots would guarantee freedom of movement for all civilians in the Kokkina and Lefka areas. Provision has been made for the movement of Turkish Cypriots from the Kokkina area under United Nations forces supervision. Finally, the entry of food and fuel into the Turkish Cypriot sector "in reasonable amounts" to be determined by the international committee of the Red Cross has been provided for, with an immediate allocation of kerosene made to relieve the present acute shortage of fuel.
The humanitarian aspect of the situation has been put in the hands of the international committee of the Red Cross, with the full backing and assistance of the United Nations peace keeping force in Cyprus.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: STATEMENT ON EXTENSION OF CHINESE ADJUSTMENT PROGRAM
speechtext:
In reply to questions raised yesterday by the hon. member for St. Paul and the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George, and following my declaration of last Friday on the adjustment statement program affecting immigrants of Chinese origin, I have reviewed the situation in the light of the experience of the last few days. I think hon. members will be interested to know that on Monday alone approximately 400 immigrants of Chinese origin came forward to regularize their status in Canada, which indicates to me that there are still a large number of this category of immigrants who have not taken advantage of this program.
In view of the above, the date of September 1 will apply only to individuals entering Canada on or after that date, and I have so advised my officials. This means in effect that the adjustment statement program will continue for the time being to apply to immigrants of Chinese origin who have entered the country previously. It seems there is a consensus that this program should come to an end. I sincerely hope the members of the Chinese community will continue to exercise their prerogatives and come forward to regularize their status. I intend to keep a close watch on the situation, and will report to the house at an early opportunity.
I will communicate the contents of my answer of today to the editors of the Chinese language newspapers in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, this house, and perhaps you yourself, sir, will have observed that except for a commendably brief and witty speech by the hon. member for New Westminster, the members of this party have not until now participated in this debate on the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City, nor indeed in the debate on the amendment since it was resumed a week ago.
This is not because we are not interested in this debate. On the contrary, we are very much interested in the debate and have definite views on the subamendment and indeed on the whole flag issue. The reason for our restraint, Mr. Speaker, is our view that an unduly prolonged debate on this subamendment, or on any other subamendment, on the amendment itself or on the main motion, would be extremely damaging to parliament and therefore to Canada itself.
Hear, hear.

Once the main issues have been made clear, continuation of debate on such an emotional subject can only serve to cause bitterness and, what is perhaps equally bad, boredom and irritation about the whole subject. I have found Canadians with a variety of opinions as to the solution of this flag question; but I have found an almost unanimous view that prolonged and repetitious debate is unnecessary and does no credit to Canada or to parliament. I do not deny the right of individual members to put their convictions on this subject on the record if they think they ought to do so, but I appeal to all hon. members, in the interests of parliament and of Canada as a whole, to do so with brevity and restraint.
It is my belief that parliament should not be in almost continuous session. One of our jobs, of course, is to debate in this house; but we have another important job, and that is to get back to our constituencies and discuss with them face to face the issues of today

Canadian Flag
and correct some of the false impressions about parliament and other public issues which are only too prevalent. As far as I am concerned, I also believe that parliament needs a reasonable recess for thought and recuperation.
As a relative newcomer to parliament I would hesitate to put forward this view were it not for the statements of a great parliamentarian whose authority, I am quite sure, will not be denied by any member here, least of all by members of the official opposition. I wish to read something said by Mr. Winston Churchill in 1931:
II you wish to say what is wrong with parliament... it is that it sits far too long in the year. I would lay down that except in times of war or great national emergency parliament should not sit more than five months, with the ordinary short intervals, say, occupying six months of the year. That ought to be the maximum.
Then again in 1944 he made a similar statement to which I call the attention of members of this house:
Do not. ..ever suppose that you can strengthen parliament by wearying it, and by keeping it in almost continuous session. If you want to reduce the power of parliament, let it sit every day in the year, one fifth part filled, and then you will find it will be the laughingstock of the nation, instead of being, as it continues to be, in spite of all the strains of modern life, the citadel as well as the cradle of parliamentary institutions throughout the world-
I should like to read another quotation from this book, which is called "Our Parliament". It is about the British parliament, and the author is Strathearn Gordon. He discusses the length of sessions and says this:
Why don't M.P.s work for more than about eight months in the year? The answer is that they do- but not at Westminster.
The same is true of Ottawa:
Most ministers undoubtedly look forward to the "holidays", when they are free from parliamentary cares, as the periods when they can put their best work into their departments.
I call this to the attention of hon. members:
But for ordinary members, too, reasonably long adjournments are a practical necessity. When a man has for many weeks been living a sort of double life, spending late nights at Westminster, speaking in his constituency at the week ends, working in the train in between, with his private affairs neglected and his nerves in shreds, it is surely right to allow him time to recuperate and think. Three hundred and seventy years ago the Lord Keeper was expressing the idea in almost lyrical Elizabethan style:
"The sessions" (he said) "cannot be long; by reason of the springtime, 'tis fit that gentlemen should repair to their countries; the justices of assize also to go to their circuits.
"So the good hours"...

I commend these words to the house; they were spoken by the Lord Keeper 370 years
ago:
"So the good hours should not be lost in idle speeches, but the little time we have should be bestowed wholly on such businesses as are needful to be considered of".
I think we should bestow our time reasonably on the sort of business that ought to be considered. There is another reason why this flag debate should not be unnecessarily prolonged and should be terminated at a reasonable time. Important as this issue of the flag is-and no one denies its importance-it is even more important that we should clear the decks of this contentious issue so we can get on with the other tremendously important business that lies before this house.
Today we mentioned the pension plan. There are many other items of legislation that ought to be dealt with. If we prolong this debate now, or put it off until some other time and resume it again, the decks will not be cleared for us to deal with that which is needful to be dealt with.
The subamendment before the house proposes a complicated plebiscite on the flag issue. I believe such a plebiscite would be divisive; I think it would be an evasion of our responsibilities as elected members of parliament. I think it would be productive of strife, bitterness and perhaps even boredom throughout the nation. I believe that we in this house were elected to take the burden of decisions in the interests of Canada as a whole. I think that if we could take a referendum, as was suggested in this house yesterday, to determine whether we should have a referendum on the flag issue, the Canadian people would tell us in no uncertain terms to do the job we were elected to do and to do it soon.
After all, Mr. Speaker, what would the referendum proposed by the subamendment solve? I suspect it would solve nothing at all. It would still leave parliament to act. Supposing, as I suggested frivolously-although it would not be funny if it in fact happened- we had a plebiscite based on the subamendment and found that 30 per cent of the people were in favour of the red ensign, 10 per cent were for the red ensign plus embellishments, 30 per cent were for a single maple leaf flag and, if I get my arithmetic right, another 30 per cent supported the three maple leaves emblem produced by the government as put before us in the main resolution. Supposing we were faced with that situation. Would the referendum have solved

anything, or would we have to renew this interminable debate all over again?
Would the hon. member permit a question? Does he believe that a preferential ballot would produce a vote such as suggested by the hon. member?

Well, I rather rule out the preferential ballot in my mind because the hon. member for Oxford, who sits on the front benches of the same party as my hon. friend and who was asked that question, said he did not think a preferential ballot was workable, and I rather accept that view. The preferential ballot would contain so many complications and difficulties that I doubt it would solve the problem.
There are far too many complications in the Pearson flag.

I think the government flag too is a little too complicated. I would prefer to see a single maple leaf.
There is another reason I suggest the subamendment should be dealt with expeditiously and rejected. It is that there is a solution available which all Canadians, or nearly all Canadians, would accept, I believe with a sigh of relief, and which would represent a non-partisan approach to the problem. This solution would be, in our view-and in this I speak for my party-to amend resolution 44A to substitute a single maple leaf design, and to amend resolution 44B to accept the Canadian red ensign as the symbol of Canadian membership in the commonwealth. The first proposal would satisfy the vast majority of the Canadian people, particularly the younger generation, who seek a distinctive Canadian flag.

Well, I know only from the letters I have received from young people and from those I speak to, and I can assure you there are a great many of them. But 1 could be wrong. What I want to say to the house is that in our view a single maple leaf design is the simplest, the strongest and the most distinctive design. Above all, if it were adopted it could not be considered as a one party approach to the problem. I know there are people in all parties, including the official opposition, who would be quite willing to accept this single maple leaf design and get rid of the stigma, if it is a stigma, of its being produced by one political party. That is not the sort of flag which perhaps we should have.

The reasons I give for accepting the Canadian red ensign as the symbol of the commonwealth in place of the union jack are these. We all respect the union jack, but it is the national flag of Great Britain. The modern commonwealth is much more than Great Britain. The Queen is the Queen of Canada as well as the Queen of Great Britain. The red ensign-and in this I may get some mild degree of support from the official opposition-as the letters received by many hon. members including myself indicate, has achieved a measure of recognition and loyalty in the hearts of many Canadians. But the solution which we propose-the adoption by this house of a single maple leaf flag as a distinctive flag for Canada, and the adoption of the Canadian red ensign as the symbol of the commonwealth-would in my judgment achieve a greater degree of acceptance than any other solution and it could be supported, as we have found out, by members of all parties in this house.
I believe the overriding consideration which should affect us all is not the views of our constituents alone, although naturally we take them into account. I believe that what should concern us most is that which will achieve the greatest measure of Canadian unity, and best serve the welfare of Canada as a whole. That is the matter which should inspire us. Therefore I urge that all of us in this house move with all reasonable dispatch, without cutting off the right of anyone who wishes to speak, but speaking with brevity and restraint, to such a solution, which I believe would find favour throughout Canada.

Would the hon. member permit a question? Would the hon. member not agree that any flag, be it the single maple leaf or some other, in order to be free from any partisan political connotation should have been recommended by a non-partisan committee with a fair degree of unanimity?

If we could start all over again I must say that I think a non-partisan committee would be a good way to start. But I do not think we can remake history. We are now well on our way into a protracted debate in this house of a matter which has been fully discussed all over the country, and I think we should deal with the propositions now before us and deal with them soon.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to congratulate all those who have taken part in this debate and who have participated in helping to define the limits within which the various political parties in this

house are dedicated to national unity. Indeed, sir, there are those who by their silence have revealed a wholesome awareness that democracy still tugs at the hearts of Canadians. It is a reminder to all of us that Canadians have a depth of feeling for and appreciation of national purpose, so much discounted by our press and by many of our fair weather politicians. I would be surprised that anyone should dare suggest that this was a matter to be disposed of in haste lest we all repent it later. I shall have something further to say later in my speech regarding the remarks made by the hon. member for Greenwood.
The forging of national unity and national purpose is no mean task requiring anybody to placidly admit or yield or concede without question the traditions of our heritage. The resolution before us authorizing a distinctive flag for Canada, with the amendment and subamendment, should have brought us to one of those happy, joyous, inspiring moments of our history. It should be a moment of mutual confidence, appreciation, trust and respect.
I say to you, sir, what a pity that is not the case today. I think of the Prime Minister, a man of reputation, a Nobel peace prize winner. I think of his zealous claims as to his devotion to diplomacy. I think of this minority government and the opportunity allowed him to share with all Canadians the choice and popularity of a national emblem. I remember the boasts made by his colleagues in his party during the election campaign that this was a man who cared about his country and its people. I think of those first few brave words of his in regard to this matter, that there would be a free vote in parliament.
Thinking of these things, sir, I also think of his threat of a general election should his party fall on this issue. I am reminded of those other careless acts committed by this government. This ill-fated parliament, born of minorities and intrigues, is witnessing another of those acts of carelessness which so vividly portray the petulance of the present Prime Minister.
We might well have overlooked that in itself, in the normal course of events had parliament been given an opportunity to fulfil the function for which it was created, the orderly dispatch of the business of this country. This measure before us was not a part of the planned program of this government for this session. Suddenly several weeks ago

That challenge came from the lips of the Prime Minister. My leader, Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, and all of us on this side of the house deplore this interruption of the business of the parliament of this country.
Oh, oh.

By the same token we on this side of the house cannot neglect our duties even in the face of the blatant threat of the Prime Minister. We have said before, and I wish to say again today, that in comparison with the urgent and vital problems facing Canadians, this appears to be a most trivial manoeuvre undertaken by the Prime Minister. There are compelling reasons, sir, to believe that this manoeuvre is the most provocative in all Canadian history. Several months ago I indicated in this house that it was apparent that this is the most careless prime minister in Canadian history. Events since then have confirmed and strengthened that belief. Indeed, a few days ago I was not surprised to hear the hon. member for Leeds credited with drawing attention to the fact that this was also a stubborn prime minister.
I ask you, sir, what has that carelessness on the part of this Prime Minister cost in terms of national unity? That question can be measured in part by the increasing cost of living borne by every household and by the multiplying burdens of those in distressed circumstances wherever they reside in Canada. That, sir, is only a small part of the cost, measured in frustration, that has been occasioned parliament, which has labelled this as one of the most unproductive parliaments in Canadian history, and which throughout its course has revealed the chief magistrate of this house as most irresponsible in the performance of his duties. The attitude taken at the time of the first Gordon budget and maintained here in the aftermath of that catastrophic event, paved the way for the present impasse.

Thank you, Mr. Speaker. When the interruption took place I was about to mention those new frontiers of development and achievement that Canadians in every part of the country are looking toward today. I wanted to say that the province of Quebec is no different from any other province in that respect, except perhaps in the

magnitude and complexity of the particular problems involved in the retention of continuity of things that are of greater importance in that part of Canada than in many other parts of the nation. I do not know why members on the government side want to deny me the right to say that, particularly the Minister of Justice.
In trying to come to the meat of the amendment and subamendment we should take a look at our history. I do not think there is a more romantic chapter in our history than that of French exploration and settlement in Canada. The church, of course, carried much of the early work in New France. In reading our history we cannot help but acknowledge the contribution made by both Protestant and Roman Catholic missionaries who were the first to recognize fully the importance and the significance of the discovery in North America.
At that time both France and Great Britain were enterprising nations competing for world commerce. The struggle for supremacy in North America is one of the intriguing stories of world history, and none of us need feel too much ashamed of the struggle that took place. Nor should we ever sell short the destiny that the results of that struggle gave to Canadians. That history is the story of the development of self-government. Nor should it ever be forgotten how tortuous the road might otherwise have been had it not been for the decision of the 13 colonies to establish an independent republic south of the border.
Indeed, sir, all of these events influenced and shaped the commonwealth of nations that is the great heritage that Great Britain will leave to the ages. I like to think that the union of French and British Canadians contributed something worth while to the development of the commonwealth as we know it today, despite the competition between the commerce, ambitions and achievements of both the mother countries.
The pioneers came to mark and hack out a new world. Many of them wanted to free themselves and future generations from the old controversies, the old traditions and old prejudices that had failed to fulfil their hopes in the lands of their origin. All of us sometimes regret the restrictions which are allowed for only a limited and somewhat token achievement of the destiny which should be ours. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that despite this fact, Canada is still a land

of hope and promise, and I am convinced it is also a land of hope and glory.
Many of the restrictions to which I have referred have been the product of compromise. During the past 97 years a new factor has enriched our national life. Thousands and thousands of new Canadians have chosen to dedicate their lives and their toil to the building of this nation. These people have come from many lands. These people have a varied background. They and their families today comprise more than a third of the population of Canada. These people are anxious to be recognized as Canadians, without any prefix or qualifications. National unity, for them, is a simple matter. They seek no special privilege. They seek only the guarantee of equality within this nation with the rest of the people of Canada. Those new Canadians who have settled in the old province of Quebec have been quick to respond to the atmosphere and environment of that province, as have Canadians who settled in other parts of the country where the response has been equally harmonious. These people recognize that more important than the origin of their neighbours is the spirit of their neighbours.
It is natural that an emerging and developing nation should have growing pains. This does not mean that our foundations should be discarded and forgotten. The founding influence of France and Britain cannot be washed from our history. It is a matter of fact. The battle of the plains of Abraham defined a new challenge for those who would inhabit the area comprising our country. The decision on Queenston heights held a measure of victory for all who claimed this territory as their home. As a consequence, French Canada was able to exert an influence in the developing commonwealth and in world affairs which might otherwise never have presented itself.

By listening to you.

I find it difficult to believe that ministers who have gone up and down this country during the last two years feeding the fires of isolation could be unconscious of the effect this would have on national unity in Canada. My sympathies are with the people of the province of Quebec. I see the cry of separation as a cry against the treachery of the Liberal party, rather than as a cry against other Canadians. The results of the actions taken by this government have been most divisive and most provocative, and I ask you, Mr. Speaker: Is this the kind of leadership we need in this country today.
Never.
Is this the action of a man who cares? Is this what we expect from a Nobel peace prize winner? Is this the policy-
No.

them, was speaking, he did not have enough courtesy to keep quiet-

It is a rule in both houses of parliament that a member must address the house orally, and not read from a written, previously prepared speech for the reason that, "if the practice of reading speeches should prevail, members might read speeches that were written by other people, and the time of the house be taken up in considering the arguments of persons who were not deserving of their attention."
It is my contention that one person has been writing most of the speeches we have heard from the other side during this debate. It is my

On the point of order, I wish to deplore the attitude of some of the members on this side of the house as well as in the other corner, as shown by the constant interruption of speakers. Mr. Speaker, you are in the chair; you are paying attention.

speechtext: Order, please. Because of the number of interruptions with which he has had to contend, I want to be fair to the hon. member and will allow him a few extra moments.

Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to thank you for your ruling. I also want to congratulate the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). He has shown himself in this house to be one backbencher across the way who does not knuckle down to the whip on that side of the house.
Hear, hear.

I might also say that I have always made my own speeches and my own notes. While I refer to notes at the present time, I make no excuse for doing so. This is a very important matter, and on the pages of Canadian history each one of us

will be recorded-what we say and what we do not say. If the hon. member for Kootenay East (Mr. Byrne) will consider that, he may think about what he should say on this occasion. The subamendment before us-

speechtext: Mr. Speaker-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Speaker. The hon. member infers that it is improper of me to draw to Your Honour's attention the fact that he is reading his speech. This is quite in order, and I still contend that the hon. member is reading his speech. I cannot prove it is not his own speech, that he did not write it, but at least I do know and can see with my own eyes that he is reading it word for word.

Mr. Speaker, the subamendment before us is an appeal for common sense. It asks the Prime Minister to consult the Canadian people as to their wishes in this regard. I ask you, sir, what request could be more reasonable than that, on a matter of such great consequence not only to us but to the generations that will follow in Canada? I ask the Prime Minister, why has he insulted parliament with his "take it or leave it" attitude, reinforced by the threat of a general election?
But there are other questions to which the handling of this matter gives pre-eminence. I ask the Prime Minister, why has he taken unto himself the choice of a national emblem design? I will deal with that design at the proper time, Mr. Speaker, if this measure is proceeded with. In the meantime I would like to put on the record my own stand made in regard to this matter on a former occasion in the House of Commons when a private member's bill was before the house. I refer to the bill brought forward by the then hon. member for St. Boniface:
I am inclined to believe that the flag of Canada should emphasize that dual personality and preserve it for future generations. This is a matter that is taking on more importance with the passage of the years. As the intermingling of the two great races, and those others included in our third dimension, are gradually and surely changing by a process of erosion and diffusion, the differences that in the beginning seemed so important are today still important because they

Canadian Flag
are giving this nation a distinctive character and personality before the world.
I referred to some of the new Canadians in these words:
Many of them fled the old lands of Europe and other continents to escape conditions and circumstances that these institutions have prevented from taking place here in Canada. To many of them the union jack will forever be a reminder of their homeland or birthplace, simply because it represented a haven here in Canada against the old established inequities which had held for them little or limited hope for the future in the land of their birth. To them a Canadian flag without some resemblance to the union jack just does not seem possible.
I went on further to say:
Whatever the design Anally approved by parliament and the Canadian people, it should be a reminder to us of our beginnings as a nation. It should reflect the part that Great Britain played in the development of our institutions. It should also reflect the personality of Canada as it has developed under the enriching influence of French culture. But more than that, it must also reflect the personality of a nation having that third dimension, that of those who chose Canadian citizenship after the destiny of Canada was decided in the articles of confederation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to make sure there are no notes on my desk from which it could be presumed that I shall be reading my speech. I am rising to take part in this debate because I feel, as many members here have expressed, this is a very, very important issue. I do not agree with those members or those people who have said this is not an important issue;

nor do I agree with those members who have accused some hon. members on the opposition side of the house of having some motive for their speeches other than that of deep concern for their constituencies and their nation.
Hear, hear.

I, for one, choose to believe, rightly or wrongly, that everyone who has taken part in this debate has done so with sincerity, integrity and believing that he represents his constituents and speaks for them. It is probably a matter of some surprise that constituents could be divided on this issue, just as this house is, but I sincerely believe this is so.
Some have said that the proposed flag was an appeasement of Quebec. We have heard a denial from the minister that the three maple leaves design was an appeasement of the province of Quebec. Possibly some hon. gentlemen do not believe the minister, but I say now that it was not an appeasement of Quebec. I am not a minister nor likely to be one. Neither have I ever said anything in this house which I did not sincerely believe to be true; and in this case I know it to be true.
Some hon. members, including the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) and others, have said that this flag will divide the country. No flag, sir, will divide a nation that is not already divided; nor will it unite a nation which prefers to live in separate solitudes.
The flag issue is not the real issue here. The subamendment is not the issue either. We are not debating here these four choices. We are not debating whether there should be a plebiscite. We are not really debating the flag. What we are really debating is our national unity* which is a matter of great importance. I think we should recognize that this is what we are really debating.
Accusing fingers have pointed to our side of the house, and it has been said that this is a matter of great excitement; that we are going to excite the people and that this is the wrong time. It is said that this is the time for reason, for calmness, for coolness, sometimes even procrastination. I for one believe in excitement if the issues involved and the theme of it is great. I believe in excitement if it helps to bring to the surface grievances which have existed for some time, and if it helps to solve them. So there is nothing wrong with excitement. As to calmness, reason-that cool, calculated sense which is desired of us-this is not going to be possible in this issue. For as I have said we are dis-

cussing our national unity. We are discussing our destiny. The real issue is our love for our country. It does not take reason to love: It takes heart and guts to love.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) made a very impassioned speech, and there is no doubt in the world that every word he uttered was a matter of great concern to him. On occasion we have to say what we have to say no matter what the cost. On occasion we have to shed a tear or a drop of blood. But we have to love our nation and the unity of our nation.
At other times we will fear for our nation and be afraid for it, and this brings me to the topic which, as I have said before, we are really discussing. We on this side have wondered how it is that so many people in Canada are staunchly entrenched behind the red ensign, a fact we did not expect, people who would otherwise have fondly and readily welcomed a new distinctive flag. It is because they are afraid, and have gathered under the ensign in fear and apprehension of one thing -the division of this nation. They fear the division and separatism about which they have heard.
Let me review for a moment some of those matters which might have given rise among Canadians in English speaking Canada to such apprehensions, which might have caused the red ensign to become the banner for English speaking reaction, as I believe it has. Let me review some of these matters, not in the light of what we see here, because we have the benefit of listening to speeches made by, for example, the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) and others, which have pointed out that separatism and division is not the clamour of most of the people in Quebec. We know that the cries for separatism and for division are really the mumblings of political idiots and charlatans. But the people of Canada who rely on the newspapers and radio for their information do not know this. They think that this is something which is desired by all of the good people in the province of Quebec. That is not so; but as I say, they do not know it. Let us consider this for a moment. Do not let us consider the acts of violence, but some of the statements of the premier of Quebec regarding the role of French culture. I recall reading in a brief presented to the federal-provincial conference that he stated it is the role, in fact the duty-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. It is of course, extremely unpleasant for the Chair to have to rise, perhaps all too often, to interrupt
Canadian Flag
hon. members in the course of their speeches, but I do feel it is my duty to remind the hon. member of the decision taken by the house the day before yesterday to the effect that, at this stage at least, remarks should be limited to the very specific aspect of the subamendment. I would therefore entreat the hon. member to relate his speech to the subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to repeat what I said at the outset, that we are not really debating the four points of the subamendment. I am saying that what is really involved is the question of our national unity, and I am trying to prove to you why. Surely you cannot deny me the right to do this. I have been referring to some of the strange statements which have been made and which might have given rise to fear and apprehension, and this matter will not indeed be solved by the four questions contained in the subamendment. These fears and apprehensions have been caused by statements made by the premier of Quebec and his ministers.
Indeed, in this very house the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Marcoux) said in a speech about education that there are two official races in Canada. What are we nonofficial Canadians to think about this? Is there some cause for concern in the rest of Canada among the six million who are supposedly non-official Canadians? I should like the house to consider the economic policies of Quebec, especially in connection with giving preference to business. I am not dealing with efficiency, but strictly provincialism. I want to review all of the things which in all fairness lead one to the conclusion that at the present time there is not a national political party in this house. I could refer, for example, to some of the strange statements made by the group on Your Honour's far left. All of this has led to apprehension and fear in Canadians. And fear for what? For national unity and for all we so vigorously seek.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that we are united, that we do have a feeling of identity and unity. Otherwise we would not be objecting. No one would object. Therefore it is our duty at this time throughout the course of this whole debate, not just when discussing the four questions, to state emphatically and irrevocably that this unity shall be preserved. Then the support behind the red ensign will fall. There is no reason for it at all except fear, and it is up to this house to show this. It is not enough to hear from the treasury benches that in all probability there will be

Canadian Flag
no separatism or division because it is not economical or feasible.
I think it was a perversion of the national feeling for the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) to recommend to this house that a committee be formed to study the effects of separatism. Division and separatism are not subjects for study, even academically. In this 97th year of our life we should be able to take for granted that this country is united and will always be united, and that there is no other choice or possibility of choice. In that way, sir, there would be no need for this subamendment or a plebiscite. There would be no need for support for the red ensign, as there obviously is at the present time.
Mr. Speaker, I have said time and time again that I do not acknowledge or recognize any form of division in this land. I should like to say that unless this House of Commons proclaims that this nation is united and that the provinces shall be united for better or for worse, and will so remain. Such action would be followed by adverse reaction, until militant action will be followed by militant reaction. At that time we would have only one choice; to choose sides and wait.
Mr. Speaker, I support a new and distinctive flag, and will do so if it comes to a vote. I support the three maple leaves design because I am not afraid of division or separatism in this country. I am not afraid because I will not tolerate such division or separatism. I will not tolerate in my mind even a suggestion of division. I would not even consider a thousand reasons produced by a special committee why separatism is feasible. I will not listen to even one member of this House of Commons who declares the possibility or advisability of separatism. I am not afraid to support the new distinctive flag on the basis of that feeling.
In conclusion may I remind hon. members of what we have done during the course of this debate, by amendments and subamendments. When the resolution was first proposed the idea caught fire from coast to coast. Every Canadian, whether naturalized yesterday, or whose forefathers have lived here for 300 years, was concerned. During this debate we have, little by little and bit by bit, abused this great idea and converted it into a plaything for all the members of this house. We have degraded this great idea and converted it into a cudgel that one right hon. gentleman may use to hammer at the head of the other. We have turned this great debate into an internal palace dialogue which only we can understand. We have left the people of Canada completely on the outside and they have

now lost patience with us. They do not understand the temper of this debate. We are going to lose their respect, as they have lost respect for this house.
I plead with all hon. gentlemen to say what they have to say in loud and clear tones. By all means, all members should express their opinions, but they should not pervert this debate by moving amendments, subamendments and more subamendments. I beg you to help in concluding this debate, so that we may give the Canadian flag back to the people, to whom it belongs.

Mr. Speaker, the few suggestions I will make to the house this afternoon, concerning the amendment and the amendment to the amendment moved in regard to motion 44(A) asking for a referendum, are not intended to extend unduly this debate, but rather to put forward the views of my constituents on the matter, as well as the views of my own party on the amendment and on the amendment to the amendment.
Mr Speaker, this debate on a really Canadian distinctive flag will, at least, have served to bring to the fore Conservative members whom we had never heard before, because yesterday, for instance, we saw and heard for the first time in the house this session the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa (Mr. Enns).
Mr. Speaker, this debate gives us an idea of what eternity will be like. Except for one or two, the speeches made by the Conservatives and their leader did nothing but pit one race against the other and they give us quite a true picture of what eternity will be like in hell.
Mr. Speaker, to say that I am against consulting our electors on important matters would not be true because with regard to the flag, I took the initiative of sending a letter to all the family heads in my riding, asking them what they thought. The 3,500 replies I received, in addition to the numerous conversations I had with people personally or by telephone every week end in my riding, enabled me to know the general opinion of my electors on that matter. Mr. Speaker, I feel that if the Conservative members had acted thus, they would not have to evade their responsibilities by calling for a plebiscite.
Some hon. members would like the motion to be referred to a parliamentary committee. In my opinion, that suggestion is unacceptable and is no solution, because the next time the

matter would be raised in the house, we would have to start all over again.
This debate has to be brought to a conclusion as quickly as possible and the problem must be solved without delay. Let us put an end to this discussion and carry on with the nation's business. We have been elected to represent our respective ridings and our countrymen. Let us discharge the responsibilities with which we have been entrusted.
For some weeks now, the administration of the country has been bogged down by the slow progress of parliament's business which is due to the systematic filibustering of the Conservatives. The house is losing considerable time listening to the empty speeches of the Conservatives who call for a plebiscite to determine whether the Canadian people are in favour of the red ensign, of a modified version of the red ensign which would include the main symbols of the two founding races, a three-leaved flag or a flag with only one maple leaf.
Why does the amendment to the amendment stop there?
Mr. Speaker, day after day and week after week, we have been getting and are still getting numerous suggestions about the flag design. Most models are quite interesting and would be truly acceptable. Why should they not be included in the referendum? Why limit the choice to four designs?
Some Conservative members told me that they would be ready to accept a flag showing the union jack, the maple leaf and the fleur-de-lis. Someone told me, one day, that a flag should not be a collection of "imperial botanical specimens" including the maple, the thistle, the rose and the lily.
Mr. Speaker, a referendum on that matter would be useless and unfair to the Canadian people; it would only divide the country even more. While the Conservatives persist in stretching the debate on the flag-
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question-
-Canadians suffer unfairly-
May I ask the hon. member a question?
Yes.

The hon. member for Chapleau said that Conservative members are bent on having this debate go on for ever. Could he tell us how many members of the Rallie-ment Creditiste have spoken in this debate so far. What percentage of the total number?
Canadian Flag
Could he tell us also whether that percentage is larger or smaller than the percentage of Conservative members who spoke on this matter?
Second question. How much time did the house spend some time ago to settle the internal problem of the Social Credit which was by far less important than the national flag issue?

Mr. Speaker, to answer the first question asked by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska, I may say that if he had intelligently followed the discussion, he would know that I am the first member of the Rallie-ment Creditiste to take the floor on the matter of a referendum, on the amendment and on the subamendment.
One thing that I find strange and quite ridiculous, is that the leader of the Conservative party moved himself an amendment to the main motion 44(A) and not being satisfied-he probably made an error and recognized it-his party moved an amendment to that amendment. That is the most ridiculous and most stupid thing I have seen in this house.
As far as the second question asked by the hon. member is concerned, I shall reply this: not only in the interest of the house, but also in the interest of the whole country, it was much more important, for the future of the nation, to ascertain where the Ralliement Creditiste should sit in this House of Commons than to discuss the flag issue as it is being discussed now.
Mr. Speaker, Canadians are going through an economic crisis comparable to that of the thirties, before the last world war. We are living through a similar crisis: the farmers and the workers, especially those in eastern Canada, are made to suffer unfairly from that situation. And the Conservatives persist in preventing measures which could remedy that situation from being presented to the house.
Unemployment is undeserved-

speechtext: Order. Could the hon. member resume his seat?
