I thank you, Mr. Speaker, for your remarks and your advice on that matter but you will admit just the same that I was led afield by the remarks made by the hon. member for Nicolet-Yamaska. Here is what I want to point out about his question of privilege. About the hon. member for Portage-Neepawa-and I checked the index of the debates of the House of Commons-I did not find his name anywhere.
Now, to revert to the subject of the subamendment, I would like to say in conclusion -not because I was intimidated by the remarks and the interjections which were made, but because I did not intend to speak at length-that Canadians-I received many letters and comments in answer to the personal inquiries I made in my riding-or most of them do not insist so much on a particular

flag design, but rather on a distinctive flag, which will represent all sections of Canada.
What Canadians ask especially is not so much a red flag, a blue flag or a white flag including all kinds of flowers or symbols one can think of, but rather a small green flag with figures on it, which would enable them to buy the things they need to give their families a decent living.
Mr. Speaker, I am convinced that instead of continuing this debate indefinitely, we should adopt the distinctive Canadian flag, settle this matter once and for all and then revert to the business of the house in order to introduce pieces of legislation likely to solve the problems facing the Canadian nation today.

On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I am told that the previous speaker said that my speech yesterday was my first intervention in debate on the floor of the house. I would merely refer the hon. member to the index of Hansard where he will see that there are some 14 or 15 entries under my name. In fact to be exact there are 22.

Mr. Speaker, it was most refreshing to hear the speech of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) today and it makes what I have to say a good deal easier. I should like to ask that member, however, to concentrate his thoughts on what is the real reason for the division in Canada today. What has brought about the trouble of the moment? There is no question in my mind that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is the prime mover behind it all. What I have to say today makes me a little annoyed, because in an offhand remark earlier today which the Prime Minister should never have made he used the word "filibuster".
Oh, oh.
Shame.

It is all right for you over there to say "shame" but I am the one who is saying "shame" and I intend to make my speech. I simply want to refer the Prime Minister to his original remarks in this debate when he emphasized the fact that he wished every member to make his contribution. To my mind it is totally unreasonable for him in an offhand way to try to deny us our rights as representatives of our constituents and to use scare tactics by referring to a filibuster. I wanted to make those comments before proceeding with my main remarks.

My purpose in speaking today is twofold. First, I believe quite sincerely that the Prime Minister has put the Liberal party in a rather poor position. My second point is that in my own humble way I would like to offer a few suggestions and if possible give him a little help, because if he does take my advice, ultimately he will be helping Canadians.
At this stage in the debate we are on the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More) which without reading it into the record, says that in any plebiscite there will be contained questions on four flags, the red ensign, a modification of it, the government's proposed flag or a modified form of the government's proposed flag.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: That is the N.D.P. proposal, the last one.

Yes, the N.D.P. proposal. The government has got itself into a rather impossible position brought about by a so-called mandate. Speaking for my own constituency, I know that no such mandate was sought. The first we heard of it was a rather long and extraordinary series of questions put to the Prime Minister with respect to a new flag. In an election these things are known to the people and eventually they trickled down to British Columbia, where the candidates were asked questions about the flag issue.
I do not know what the Liberal members now in the house said they would do, but I just wonder how the Liberal party can claim in any way shape or form that it actually got a mandate from the people on the flag issue. Prior to the election the Liberal party published advertisements in the newspapers in British Columbia outlining the policy it would follow if returned to office. I shall not make reference to all the things they said they would do, and later on said they would do in 60 days, but have not done. I am looking at this published manifesto of the Liberal party and no reference was made in British Columbia to a new flag. What I have in my hand is a full page advertisement from the Victoria Colonist of March 31, and nothing about the ensign was mentioned in it.
However as I have said the news trickled down into British Columbia, and at the election meetings which were attended by the four candidates-Liberal, New Democratic party, Conservative and Socred-we were asked, and I remember it so well, "If a new flag is proposed, would you do away with the red ensign?" The Liberal candidate replied, "You 20220-445
Canadian Flag
will throw away the red ensign over my dead body."

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: That fellow isn't here.

He isn't here now, but he was a good Liberal. You may make your speech in your own time. Often enough you read your little book and point out "We shouldn't really interrupt the person who has got the floor and is speaking." My Liberal opponent spoke a lot more sensibly than some members opposite, and said they would only do away with the red ensign over his dead body.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

No; afterwards if you like. The government has got itself into a ridiculous position with respect to the red ensign, a position that is untenable.
The second point I wish to make is in reference to the feelings of people in my own constituency. I have received many letters, and a preponderance of them were in favour of the red ensign. In fairness I say I have received some in favour of the government proposal, others who would like a modification of the government proposal and others still who say, "Let us look for another flag altogether." The opinions expressed in the letters were backed up by those I received as I went through my riding.
With regard to polls, I would like to quote from the Penticton Herald which conducted a local poll as a direct result of the clamour that was going on over the flag issue. This is the issue of the Herald for June 10 last and the heading is, "For ensign 89 per cent."
Almost 90 per cent of all those Herald readers who voted in the flag poll which ended last Saturday backed the red ensign, and this surely is significant. Many red ensign backers even went to the limit in their vehemence by defacing the ballot coupon provided for readers supporting Pearson's maple leaf flag. One reader scrawled across the maple leaf side-"No, no, a thousand times no, I'd rather die than say yes." But most ensigners simply cast their ballot without emotional embellishment.
There is a lot more in this report which is not very favourable to the Liberal party, dealing with the manner in which the flag issue was introduced, but I shall not read that.
We have also had independent Canadian polls, and when I heard the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) say the vast majority of people favour the new flag I thought he might have dropped dead in his tracks. If he knew anything about polls he would know

Canadian Flag
that in eight out of nine provinces there is a preference for the red ensign.
I next wish to deal with the so-called free vote. These are points on which the government has got itself so far out on a limb that it must do something, and I will have suggestions to make later which I think will be helpful. When you consider a free vote it looks nice. The Prime Minister is a great man for making nice statements right off the bat. The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Coates) asked him a question on May 12 as reported at page 3164 of Hansard. He asked: What about a free vote; are you going to give us one? Those are not the hon. member's exact words but that is the substance of the question. And the Prime Minister replied-[DOT] and these are his exact words:
When the time comes to submit the decision of the government in this matter to the House of Commons I would hope every member of the house would vote as his conscience dictates and that there would be no question of confidence or non-confidence in a party sense.
That is fine. Everyone would say: the Prime Minister is a good boy. It will be a free vote and no party whips will be in evidence. The right hon. gentleman changed that pretty quickly. I think someone else started to talk to him. Anyway, a week later, on May 19, the Prime Minister said the government would stand or fall on the flag question. Well, I sure hope they fall flat on their faces, because, boy, do they deserve it! They have done a most divisive thing. The hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto) was talking over there, and I liked some of the things he said, but he slithered over one little thing. He did not bring out why we were having this divisive thing at the present time. He said Canada is great, we are all here; there is no division; we should all pull together. I agree with him 100 per cent. But he missed one point. The Prime Minister has brought this question before the House of Commons and in all petulancy he says: A free vote? Nothing doing, boys, you are going to sit here until this thing is voted upon. Furthermore, you are going to miss your holidays. Mr. Speaker, I enjoy holidays as much as anyone else though I do not regard time spent in my constituency as a holiday, but rather as a chance to get to know the views of the people in my riding. That is one of the sensible things the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) said this afternoon. I think we would all like to get home, not as I said to have a holiday, but to keep in touch with our constituents.

The hon. member also said a rather silly thing. He said we should be getting on with the other business of this house. I am sorry. We have finished the business which was proposed by the Prime Minister and by the leader of the house over there. We have finished every last scrap with the exception of this flag question. I remind hon. members that we have finished the other business which was before us, and now we should sit until we have finished this, regardless of how long it takes and regardless of loose statements such as the one made by the Prime Minister today regarding a filibuster.
I mentioned the divisive effects of this issue. Many people have spoken on this subject. It is a matter of opinion, depending on what one stands for, how it is treated in this house. There are two sides to every question, but apparently, there are five sides here. 1 feel strongly enough on this subject to be willing to sit here all through the summer and through the fall if necessary. I couldn't care less, because I feel I am right and that I am speaking for my constituents and for a great many more.
Hear, hear.

Let us not divide Canada. Last night I was feeling a little blue because I could not get on the list, there were so many extra speakers. I went upstairs and just before six o'clock I was having a talk with a friend. I asked the question: Who do you think is winning in this flag debate? And he gave me a very sensible answer. He said in answer to my question: Do you think anyone is winning? From that point on we began to discuss the effect of this flag debate on Canada. I rather liked his remarks. They were good. Let us not worry about winning in the House of Commons; let us start worrying about what is happening in our various constituencies throughout Canada.
Who would have thought when we got into this flag debate we would have seen such a variety of feeling? May I quote from an article entitled "Another Slant on Flag Issue" written by the Rev. A. V. Bentum, pastor emeritus of St. Andrew's presbyterian church, Penticton. He is not a man of my faith, but he is a man I respect, and I quote from this article because of its acute and reasoned assessment of certain qualities to which we as Canadians in many instances pay only lip-service. The article is a little long but I think it is necessary for me to read it at this time.
Few would have suspected, when Mr. Pearson in his election speeches promised to do something in the matter ol a distinctive flag lor Canada.

that it would have provoked such a variety of feelings when implemented. One cannot help feeling, nevertheless, that it is good to have these feelings brought out where we can look at them.
A large number of Canadians may feel that the matter is a "storm in a teacup". Some have said that they "couldn't care less". Such an attitude is as much to be deplored as the one which rabidly and unreasoningly takes sides. The flag is a symbol of the feeling which binds us together as a people.
No matter how much we may desire to expand nationalism into the wider internationalism, we shall not succeed unless we can learn to feel something positive for each other in the smaller groups. In a culture which exhibits a trend to the impersonal, one becomes apprehensive of this "couldn't care less", attitude. It is, unfortunately, all too prevalent.
Again, there are some who regard the attitude of these Canadian veterans who prefer the red ensign as reactionary, obscurantist and die-hard. The feelings of this group of citizens should not be sneered at, or passed lightly over.
Ties which have bound men together, especially in grim situations and circumstances, are not easily broken or cast aside. Those who have never lived outside the security of their own land cannot know the feelings which such a symbol as a flag can evoke.
We appear to be living in a day and generation when loyalty and veneration for anything, except oneself, is all too rare. Displays of positive sentiment may be considered weak or outmoded. Chivalry and courtesy belong to the dead past.
yiolent and destructive feelings are more in evidence in many groups and areas of the world. There seems to be a rebellion against tradition and authority, which could be useful if constructively directed, but with it there seems to go a rejection of discipline.
That very word implies regard for others, since it comes from the same source from which we get the word 'disciple'.
There may be something intriguing about "sweeping the board clean", as it were, and starting out with an entirely new flag design. Is this attitude not too consistent with what we have been saying; the apparent desire to disown one's own history?
Some sections of our society find their ideals and leadership in their own peer groups. They do not want any part with ancestors or past history.
The end results of this are to be seen in the often-lacking idealism, and the failure to profit by past experience, which is really historical perspective.
We in Canada are not a nation without ancestors, past history or historical ties. It must surely be part of a nation's strength to foster and preserve these. It may be the lack of them which causes new nations and cultures to go to emotional excesses in trying to find causes and binding ties. Those nations which have shown strength in the past have usually been the ones which have had respect for ancestors, and venerated their own history.
One hopes that we in Canada, while adding new chapters, through new sons and daughters both natural and adopted, will not discard the heritage that is ours, in a willingness to appear modem, by being cynical about sentimental attachments to the past.
Canadian Flag
Whether the red ensign should be the flag for Canada or some other, need we obliterate all reference to the cultures which have played such a large part in the making of the nation?
A truly Canadian flag need not be less Canadian in character should it show in its composition some relationship to the flags which so many sons and daughters have loved, fought under and for which they have lived and died.
I am glad I have read that to the house.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: May I interrupt for one moment?
Absolutely. I do not mind.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: When the hon. member began his remarks he indicated that they would be related to the subamendment and I am just wondering whether he is not departing now, to some extent, from that purpose.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad you let me finish putting that on the record. As I said at the beginning of my remarks, this government has got the country in an uproar, and I want to try and do something to help this situation. I related this to the fact that the mandate which was given out with regard to the red ensign-which is No. 1 on the plebiscite-was never a mandate in my riding; it was never a request by this government. In fact, it was directly and distinctly, on more than one occasion, denied by the Liberal candidate who ran against me in the last election. Incidentally, this flag question was raised during a previous election campaign; I believe in 1962. Like many other members in this house at that time, particularly those from British Columbia, I believe there was a denial that the red ensign would ever be taken away from Canada. Have I much time left, Mr. Speaker?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I might advise the hon. member that according to the record I have from the table he has until ten minutes after five o'clock.

Thank you very much, Mr. Speaker. I do not intend to take the full time because I believe I have pretty well covered what I wanted to say. I will now deal with the choices which are offered by this plebiscite, and I want to talk particularly about the red ensign. The red ensign is not a new flag, as some people would have us believe.
I do not wish to read too much material into the record, but we all know that up to 1904 -when we had a Liberal government also- the red ensign fluttered over these parliament buildings. It had been flown on parliament hill from the time of confederation until 1904. It is a flag which over a long period of time

Canadian Flag
*-ever since I can remember-I have felt was my own flag, and my friends felt the same way. We used to put it up on my house on May 24, I remember so distinctly. There was never any question that it was Canada's flag. However, in 1904 somebody, on orders from the Liberal party, ran up the union jack. Questions were asked in the house, and finally the ensign, which had been hauled down, was put up again. Canadians had come to regard the red ensign as their flag.
In this connection I often think of one or two men for whom I have a fair regard. I do not mind saying that. An old fraternity brother of mine, Right Hon. Mackenzie King, had no illusions about changing this flag or, I think, about the diversity it would cause in Canada. In fact, when talking to General Crerar when he came back after the war and they drove up to the parliament buildings, he said, "General Crerar, your soldiers have decided one thing; that is, Canada's flag". He was referring to the red ensign which was flying over the parliament buildings. There is another man who many of us feel was a responsible citizen. He was a prime minister of this country, and his name is Louis St. Laurent. That right hon. gentleman said, when approached on the subject of a new flag, that he would not introduce a new flag because it would be too divisive of Canada.
I say, Mr. Speaker, that the feeling that was evident throughout Canada at that time is the feeling that should be evident today. This is a divisive subject. I agree with the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto), although I may differ as to the end result. The hon. member said we should take a new flag and, quite frankly, I think that was the one fault in a rather good speech. I do not think we should take a new flag at the present time.
When?

An hon. member said, "When". There could come a time when this is necessary, and no one should ever close the door for ever and ever on any change whatsoever in respect of a nation. My own views on the flag are well known in my constituency. I stand for the red ensign and I have made no bones about this. I think the first letter I received in parliament was asking my views on the red ensign-this goes back to 1958- and I answered that letter just as I have answered every similar letter I have received, whether they have been for or against the red ensign. I always say I stand for the red ensign.

I said, Mr. Speaker, there were two matters that I wanted to bring out in my speech. The first was that this government has got this country into an unholy, divisive mess. Consequently I believe this is a time for a little wisdom to be shown and I wish to offer one or two suggestions. I believe that the flag issue is far too explosive to be decided now. In my opinion the whole question should be stayed pending a very thorough and more mature consideration of this question. This is a time for an appeal to common sense. A plebiscite should finally be held.
I am not in agreement that we should put everything on this plebiscite, in whatever way, shape or form; but I suggest that a parliamentary committee, or a joint committee of the House of Commons and the Senate, be held, and that the previous findings of the earlier committee on this subject should be considered. Incidentally, they were rather fine findings. However, they should be considered by the committee, and it should take a little time on this matter. They should go into everything that has happened in this regard since then, and should pay a little attention, perhaps, to this b. and b. deal that is running around Canada-not that I think much will come out of that. In any event, the committee should consider the results that come out of this royal commission.
Having used the word "finally" in regard to a plebiscite, I would say the committee's findings and recommendations should be put in the form of a plebiscite, preferably containing as few flags as possible. This plebiscite should then be put to the people of Canada. This is my suggestion, Mr. Speaker. It has been made before, but it is one I have felt right from the beginning was a proper suggestion.
I do not think a flag should be forced on Canada. This issue is too highly political in nature and it is divisive in the extreme. In my opinion Canadians should never have been put in this position. Let us not have a "take it, or else" flag. Now is the time-and I am using the words of the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) last evening-for a responsible course to be taken by a responsible statesman. We have in this house different points of view, different forms of approach; and believe me, Mr. Speaker, this is not a time for railroading something through. This is a time for extreme caution, not because of the flag alone but also because of the dangerously explosive situation which exists in Canada. The flag is only one mani-

festation of this explosive situation. We hope that when a flag is decided upon it will be with us forever, and this is no time for undue haste.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to participate in this debate 1 make no apologies to anyone. In fact, it would appear that the time is fast approaching when those members who do not participate are the ones who are going to have to make apologies, not only in this House of Commons but in their home ridings as well.
In the riding I represent, Middlesex East, I have well over 100,000 sincere Canadian citizens. I am well aware that not all of them favour either side in this issue. I have had many letters from constituents, the large majority of them in favour of the red ensign. Many are in favour of a distinctive Canadian flag; but I have yet to receive one in favour of the Pearson pennant. How can the government of Canada deny to the people of this country the right to express their opinion, as requested by the amendment and the subamendment which have been proposed in this house? Frankly, I favour the retention of the red ensign. This is not unreasonable because I have a typical Canadian background and ancestry.
What is that?
When I say that, I am referring to Scots-Irish. I make no apology. Nor do I belittle any other ancestry in this country.
What about the Indians?

What about them? Are hon. members opposite going to give them a chance to express their views on the flag issue? I think it is true that in every constituency in Canada there is a division of thought. I do not think there is any member in this House of Commons who could stand up and say that all his constituents were in favour, one way or the other. How, then, can the government take a stand and say to the people: "This is what you will have as a flag. This is what you will accept; take it and like it"? This does not make sense. How can this minority government-and I repeat "minority government"-force their choice of a flag on the people of Canada? Is this their interpretation of democracy?
It is quite true that the government of the day would have us believe that they carry a mandate to introduce a new flag in this country. Nothing could be further from the truth. The present Prime Minister came to
Canadian Flag
the city of London during the last election campaign and spoke to a group of over 5,000 people-a Liberal estimate, Mr. Speaker. During his speech to all these sincere Canadians the fact that this government contemplated the destruction of the red ensign was never mentioned. It is very difficult, as many speakers have said, to find any reference to destroying the red ensign and replacing it with another flag. However on turning to the Globe and Mail, in a report which carries a quotation from Winnipeg some time in April, 1963 this appears:
Liberal leader Lester Pearson yesterday rejected the red ensign as Canada's official flag. He told a group of editors of ethnic newspapers that a distinctive Canadian flag should be one that could not be mistaken for the emblem of any other country.
Why did the Prime Minister not tell that to the 5,000 people he spoke to in London, Ontario, if it was part of his platform? It is one thing to promise a distinctive Canadian flag, but it is quite another to come to this parliament and say: "We have decided the flag that the Canadian people will have. This is what we have chosen for you: accept it and like it. Should this house not accept that flag we will be faced with an election".
Parliament will decide, not this party.
Yes, with a free vote and a Liberal majority.
No, there is no Liberal majority.
Look at your friends to the left. There is no question where they stand.
They are supporting us.

I cannot help but think how interesting it will be when the next election comes along and the Liberals, the N.D.P. and the Ralliement Creditistes are all taking the platform and claiming credit for introducing the new flag. I never saw such a group of M.P.s so determined to commit political suicide as we have in the left hand corner of this house. I am wondering whether they are labouring under the illusion that the Liberal party will withdraw the Liberal candidates in their ridings.
If I may return to the Globe and Mail- and I think I am getting back to the subamendment-
About time.

I do like to hear these interjections from the other side because it indicates that one is getting close to the truth. And it

Canadian Flag
really hurts sometimes. If I may refer again to the Globe and Mail, Mr. Speaker, it does appear that there is still one Tory who writes for that newspaper who has not yet received the hatchet treatment. I refer of course to the columnist Mr. Bruce West, who remains loyal to the red ensign and is not afraid to say so, for which I give him credit. Bruce West in his column for Thursday, August 13, sums up the whole flag issue in one sentence when he says:
I am sure that many of us who now oppose the scrapping of our present proud flag would be willing to shut up and bow to the will of the majority if a referendum indicated that a new flag were desired by this country.
Further to that, Mr. Speaker, I should like to state my own position, which is simply this. If the people of Canada indicated by a referendum, by a free vote, that they were in favour of any one particular design, I would be prepared to accept that design without even seeing it. This, I believe, is democracy. The majority should rule.
The blind leading the blind.
That is what you would have us believe.
You are hardly supporting the red ensign.
Why doesn't the hon. member stand up and say that?
Yes, I will do that. I say to my hon. friend that he does not stand up so much for the red ensign when he speaks like that, saying that he will accept any flag.
What I said was that I myself prefer the red ensign; but if the majority of the people of Canada indicate that they want something else, then I will accept that.
A majority of the house.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Let us have a look at it.

It will be the will of the majority. We have to sit and look at you, and you represent the majority.
Mr. Speaker, this is the whole question. What proof is there that the people of Canada want a new flag? What indication has there been of this fact? If the Prime Minister is as brave as he would have us believe, why does he not go to the people of Canada and give them an opportunity to express their opinion? I would love to see some of the hon. members opposite, particularly those from English speaking ridings, squirm when this flag issue is brought up at the next election.
I did not squirm.
You may squirm the next time.
What other word could you use to describe it?

If the Prime Minister is convinced that the people of Canada are so anxious for a new flag, he should have no fear of providing them with an opportunity to so indicate by a vote; or is it a fact that the Prime Minister, in his manoeuvring, would like to solidify certain necessary elements of support before he takes that gamble?
It is time, Mr. Speaker, that the people of Canada were informed that this flag issue is not holding up the business of this country, or the business of parliament. The Prime Minister himself stood in this House of Commons this afternoon and said that he hoped the flag debate can be terminated so we can consider a well earned recess, and then return to this house and take up the pension legislation and other important business. Why does the press, as well as many other individuals, attempt to lead the people of Canada to believe that we are obstructing the business of this house and this country when it is a fact, as corroborated this afternoon by the Prime Minister, that the business of this session is now completed?
It is openly admitted inside and outside of this house that many people object to placing the union jack on any part of a distinctively Canadian flag. My question, Mr. Speaker, is this: Why were those same people so strangely silent at the time they were happy to accept the protection of the union jack in two world wars? There is no answer to that question.
The union jack and the red ensign represent the basic freedoms everyone in this country enjoys. Those flags denote the reason why many people from all over the world have chosen to come to this country and take the oath of citizenship under the red ensign. Should we be ashamed to display the red ensign as part of any flag of Canada? The answer to that question is no. Should we be ashamed to have the red ensign as part of any Canadian flag? The same answer applies to that question. Should we destroy parliament itself simply because it is patterned after the mother of parliaments at Westminster? If that reasoning is good on one side it must be good on the other side. This must also apply to our whole system of justice.

The whole purport of the amendment, as moved by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), and the subamendment, as moved by the hon. member for Regina City (Mr. More), is to give the people of Canada an opportunity to express their feelings and wishes. I think that is a democratic practice and we on this side of the house are in support of it.
Mr. Speaker, would the hon. member permit a question?
Certainly.
Can the hon. member indicate to this house any democratic country that has adopted a flag through the procedure which has been suggested by the hon. member?

I cannot name any country that has done this, but how many countries have had a flag shoved down their throats by one Liberal party? I shall go further, how many countries have had a flag forced upon them by the Prime Minister and a man such as he who is on his feet?
Does the hon. member remember the fashion in which the interim flag that has prevailed since 1945 was selected? It was done by order in council.
I support this flag because it is a flag that I love.
Are you going to impose your flag?
This flag has already been imposed, and it was a Liberal government that imposed it on the country. I am prepared to accept it. I refer of course to the red ensign.
Would the hon. member for Middlesex East permit a question?
Yes.

My question is prompted by t.v. commercials. Does the hon. member realize that the remarks being made by the Minister without Portfolio (Mr. Dupuis) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) can be likened to television, where there are more commercials than programs?
I should like to thank the hon. member for his question, but remind him that this condition is normal.
The hon. members are enjoying themselves.

This government is the only government in the history of politics that has
Canadian Flag
29 different speakers, and every time someone on this side of the house makes a remark they object to, 27 of those speakers shout "order, order". They have not the nerve to stand up on their feet and say what they have to say, but hide behind their hands.
Shame.
We love that sort of performance, and we are used to it.
I had 50 members interrupting me yesterday.

You are an outstanding speaker. Mr. Speaker, I should like to state I enjoyed the speech made by the Minister of Trade and Commerce, but I do not like his attitude when he attempts to convince us that the government has made a decision for us and that we should say nothing more. I do not like his suggestion that the government has made a recommendation, and the Liberal party can make no mistakes, and that we accept their recommendation and keep quiet. I refuse to follow that suggestion.
I intend to conclude my remarks, Mr. Speaker-
Oh, no.

I am sorry to disappoint the hon. member for Northumberland (Miss Jewett). I suggest she would do well to spend some time in her own riding in an attempt to discover the feeling of the Canadian people there whom she is supposed to represent.
I just came back from there.
I hope you have, and I hope to see you here after the next election.
I have news for you.

Mr. Speaker, in the entrance hall in front of this chamber there is a bronze statue in honour of one Lieutenant Colonel George Harold Baker, a member of parliament, who gave his life in defence of this country. As a part of this memorial there is a stone tablet upon which is carved a verse from probably the best known of all Canadian poems, which reads as follows:
To you from failing hands we throw The torch: be yours to hold it high.
If ye break faith with us who die We shall not sleep, though poppies grow In Flanders fields.
That was not the red ensign.

Just listen Moe, and you will get it.

Canadian Flag
Mr. Speaker, to many Canadians, including myself, that torch is symbolized in the Canadian red ensign. I say that this government is breaking faith with every man or woman who has ever served in armed forces of Canada.
Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, if this resolution is forced through the House of Commons, then the government should commission the stonemasons working on the building to destroy that tablet, because under this legislation it becomes a mockery.
Thank you.
Mr. Speaker, it is obvious that not much new can be contributed to this debate-
Hear, hear.

-by a humble backbencher like myself. However, like the previous speaker I make no apology whatsoever for getting to my feet and taking the time of the house. It is my right and my duty as an elected representative, and I am merely acquiescing in the invitation extended to me by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) of this country. I should like to pause for a second and ask: Who is there in this house to deny me the right to voice my opinion?
No one.
Who is?

The Prime Minister
invited us to speak. Yet this afternoon he referred to our participation as a filibuster. Be that as it may, I say in all humility that I hold the forlorn hope that in my humble way I might suggest something that could bring, so far as the greatest number of people in Canada are concerned, a happy solution to this impasse. I should like to say that whatever flag is chosen for this great dominion of ours I will honour and revere it.
Hear, hear.

Furthermore, to put hon. members' minds at ease may I say I intend to heed the counsel of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) who suggested this afternoon that perhaps we should be brief.
I have examined in some detail most of the speeches that have been made in this so-called flag debate. Last Wednesday the hon. member for Grey-Bruce (Mr. Winkler) led off and the purport of his remarks was to the effect that we should deport ourselves like gentlemen and members of parliament. Other hon. members have suggested that we should have a free vote. In my humble opin-

ion the fact is that at the present time this is an impossibility because the political machine has whipped the boys into line and I do not honestly think that a free vote could be held.
A further suggestion that appears in reading some of the speeches is that the government might appoint a joint committee of both houses to study the situation. It has also been evident in practically every speech that has been made that there is a heartfelt desire on the part of every member that we should do our utmost to build unity in this country. Another good suggestion was made by the hon. member for Greenwood this afternoon, and I believe he quoted Winston Churchill as his authority. He suggested that members should be allowed to go home and discuss the situation with the people.
Every speech that has been made has contained certain common denominators, first a plea to achieve unity, and second a plea to remove the flag from party politics. Another common thought that has been expressed is that we should let the people themselves decide, as they should in a democracy. This thought is contained in every speech I have read, with the notable exception of one. I was disappointed, indeed I was dismayed, that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) was the only one who did not have in his remarks-at least, it was not apparent to me-any idea that the people themselves should decide. His was an unswerving, dictatorial attitude with no give and take. His was the only speech I could discover in which the speaker actually referred to appeasement of Quebec.
I discovered something else in going through these speeches and it is something I do not particularly like, something that pains me a little. I refer to the fact that in so many places references have been made to the Prime Minister and he has been described as being autocratic, petulant, domineering and arrogant because, they say, of his insistence on a vote on the flag before a recess. I do not share these sentiments. I do not believe a man could become prime minister of this country and leader of a large political party unless he was a man of some stature. However I do believe that the Prime Minister is listening to bad advice from some cocky, opinionated advisers and if he persists in continuing to listen to them I feel he must be held responsible. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, this government has no reason to be arrogant or cocky. They have no mandate to force their will on the public. They should listen

to the voice of the people. The government is in just about the same position as I am personally.
Bankrupt?

No, Mr. Speaker, not bankrupt financially, although I must admit I am not blessed with too much of this world's goods. However, the government is in the same position as I am so far as a mandate is concerned. When I get feeling too big for my britches and start to feel quite important as a member of this house, I turn my mind back to the election in April and rediscover the fact that I was elected by the large majority of 24 votes over my closest opponent. Now, this is not the point. In the election there were 931 more votes cast against me than for me, and those people who did not vote for me are entitled to their opinion and I believe I should endeavour at least to consider their viewpoints. This, Mr. Speaker, I propose to do so long as I am able.
I intend to try and be a representative of the people of my constituency and to be considerate of all of them. I would recommend this course to the present government because it is in exactly the same position as I, so far as a mandate is concerned, only it is worse percentagewise. I must realize that out of almost 8 million people casting votes, only 3J million cast votes for the Liberal party. For these reasons I say consideration and moderation should be the approach of the Liberal party to the flag issue.
Now, Mr. Speaker, heeding the advice of the hon. member for Greenwood (Mr. Brewin) I intend to conclude, and I have just this one last thought to leave with you. I say to the Prime Minister that this is a time for greatness. This is a time for him to stand for democracy. This is his opportunity to rebuff those phony advisers who are leading him down the garden path to oblivion. I say, Mr. Prime Minister, make your own decisions; appoint a committee or have a referendum; do something which will give the people of Canada a democratic chance to pick out their own symbols divorced from party politics.

I have listened to the hon. gentleman's speech very carefully and I would like to ask a question of clarification. Was he advocating a plebiscite or a committee of this house, of members of parliament, to make a decision on the flag? I was not sure which.

If the minister will read my speech tomorrow he will see that the door was left open for either one.
Canadian Flag

Mr. Speaker, on entering this debate for the second time I first wish to comment on the contributions made by hon. members to date. It is my considered opinion that the calibre of the speeches delivered has been of the highest quality during this debate, in fact the highest since I took my seat in 1957. There is good reason for this high calibre. It is because hon. members who have been speaking have been speaking from their hearts, have been speaking with a feeling that is only evident when speaking about symbols that represent your country, your history and your tradition.
We have heard many complaints from newspapers in this country, through their editorial writers, that too often speeches in the House of Commons are as dull as ditch-water and thus unfortunately, too many newspapers have reached a decision to print little or nothing of what is being said in the house on this important matter. I ask, when has the point been reached that the newspapers of this country make an assessment beforehand of what their readers should see and what they should consider?
If the newspapers of this country were realistic, if they were to go out into any group in any area of this country and sit down and talk with the people, they would find that no issue is more important or more discussed at present than this specific flag issue. I have discussed this issue with many people in many areas, and as a result of my discussions I wish to pose certain questions to the Prime Minister in the hope that he might, when he has the opportunity, take his seat in the house and give answers to these questions.
Order paper.
My friend, if you consider this is the type of thing that should go on the order paper then I say, sir, you should not be allowed to sit in the House of Commons.
I will resign then.

I believe the time has arrived when the Prime Minister must reconsider the position in which he has put the House of Commons on this important matter, for I am sure all members will agree that this debate has far reaching implications for the future of our nation. Many have contended that an election campaign based on this volatile issue would not be in the best interests of the nation. Accepting this as a correct premise, I ask the Prime Minister to consider what is

Canadian Flag
happening in parliament now, and if this is really a substitute for an election campaign that is of benefit to our future?
I ask him this, sir, because no matter what is said in the house, he is the Prime Minister of the country; he is the man who determines what we debate and when we debate it. He can talk about meetings of party leaders all he desires but he is still the man who runs this country, or is supposed to be running it at this time.
I ask the Prime Minister if he does not believe that the flag design which he proposes as an alternative to the Canadian red ensign is not the type of design that will offend a large number of Canadians in every province of this nation? The Prime Minister in proposing this design suggested that we should have a resolution authorizing the flying of the union jack as an alternate design. It was his hope that those who would be offended would derive some consolation from the second flag.
May I ask the hon. gentleman where he gets the idea that this is an alternative flag?
I beg your pardon.
Where is your authority for saying this is an alternative flag?

Mr. Speaker, if the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) will wait I think I will indicate it to him. It has to be an alternative flag. There cannot be two flags flying from every flag pole in this nation. Let us be realistic. One flag.
One Canadian flag.

Right. I say to the hon. gentleman: Is this really an honest approach to the flag question? Can there be any assurance that any second flag which may be adopted will become a part of our Canadian nation for any length of time? The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) in his speech outlined what transpired in relation to a second flag in South Africa. Would this not also be the history of a second flag in Canada?
Now, I ask this question: Who is deriving the greatest pleasure from the action taken by the government on the flag issue? I suggest to the Prime Minister that he is providing a degree of pleasure for the separatists in the province of Quebec which they are not worthy of deriving. He has also produced a degree of extremism among many loyal Canadians throughout the nation which makes future Canadian unity a questionable subject. Does

the Prime Minister want a flag which will aggravate the feelings of large sections of the population? Do French Canadians generally consider a flag design satisfactory when it will displease large sections of the population? I do not for one moment consider they wish any such result. Indeed, except for the vociferous separatist element in the province of Quebec I find little to indicate how the sensible and realistic Canadian in that province feels about this flag issue. I ask the Prime Minister to tell me how the good citizens in the province of Quebec who desire a united and progressive nation feel about Canada's flag. Surely, there must be some method of determining how the people of that province feel with regard to its design, or with regard to a design which would have an association with our history and traditions.
Would the hon. member permit a question? Has he inquired of his own members from the province of Quebec to get an answer to those questions?

I certainly have and I find there is a degree of responsibility indicated in their replies to me which has certainly not been evident among the members on his side representing the same province, as indicated by the interjections they make every time-

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. Perhaps I can take advantage of the interruption by the minister to inform the hon. member that he is obliged to direct his remarks to the subamendment. The hon. member is in a particular situation inasmuch as he has already participated in the debate; he spoke on June 17 last in connection with the amendment. Today, of course, he is speaking on the subamendment. It is a basic rule of this house that a member can only speak once on a question. It is in order, of course, to speak a second time on the subamendment, but surely any speech at this stage should be relevant to the new question and not to the old question on which he has already spoken.

Thank you. I think Your Honour will have no difficulty in finding that I will be speaking on the subamendment before the house.
I support the contention that the government has mishandled the flag issue so badly that it is not possible now to make a realistic appraisal of the subject within the confines of the House of Commons. Once it became a government measure, the flag design proposed by the Prime Minister became a government flag. It became a flag closely associated with the Liberal party. Such a flag

has little hope of acceptance among those who do not adhere to Liberal philosophy in this nation. Indeed there are many who have adhered to the Liberal philosophy who cannot associate that philosophy with the design presently proposed. For this reason it would appear to be best for the nation if a plebiscite were held, since, apparently, this is the only means of taking the flag issue out of partisan politics.
At the same time it seems to me that in reaching a conclusion as to what the new flag design should contain the government has attacked this problem in reverse order. Would it not have been more sensible to have assumed that a large proportion of the Canadian public favours the Canadian red ensign? Before producing a new flag design, they should have assumed that this support was present and, in order to develop a new design which would inspire an even greater acceptance, they should have tried to evolve a design based on the Canadian red ensign- a flag which would have embodied in it an association with our history and tradition, as well as symbols which are not now contained therein but which could be developed in a new flag without making a complete break with the past.
I would have thought the government's study of the great flag debate in South Africa if it did nothing else, would have provided it with sufficient experience and knowledge to appreciate that the people of a nation, especially a nation which is bicultural in character, would not allow the rights of either a large minority or a small majority to be trampled upon. When this occurs, as is demonstrated in Canada today, only the extremists derive pleasure from the results of the decision.
As members of this house are aware, I have been a strong advocate for the retention of the Canadian red ensign. So long as this government considers that the only alternative available to the Canadian red ensign is their own proposed flag design I shall fight their action by every means at my disposal. If these two designs are the only alternatives which must be decided upon, then I feel I am doing my duty as a Canadian in avoiding a proposal which would destroy and eliminate any association between the flag of our nation and our history and tradition. At the same time, if the government were to indicate that they were endeavouring to introduce a flag design which would be more acceptable to the great majority of Canadians in all parts of this nation, a design which 20220-4464
Canadian Flag
would also have an association with our history and tradition, then I would be the first to try to assist that government in arriving at a satisfactory conclusion.
Among all the letters I have received from every part of this nation I have found few whose authors, though they confirmed their belief that the Canadian red ensign should remain as our flag, were not also willing to concede that they would agree to alterations in that flag which would give greater recognition to the bicultural character of our nation as long as the union jack remained as a continuing symbol of the contribution we have received from our connection with the British commonwealth of nations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: It is called the commonwealth of nations, now.
It is kind of you to correct me.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: You should know.
As far as I am concerned it is still the British commonwealth of nations.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext: We know that perfectly well. It is obvious.
Surely this house cannot continue indefinitely-
Certainly not.

-with a debate of this type. Surely, at some time, the government must realize that we have to reach a conclusion which will end the debate. To date, the government has been adamant that this house must accept the flag they have produced or else debate forever.
May I ask a question?

I am not going to answer a question right now. Surely it is not the responsibility of the Leader of the Opposition or of any of the opposition party leaders, but it is the responsibility of the Prime Minister of this nation-
Which he is discharging.

No, he is not discharging it. I cannot agree with that at all. He is not discharging his responsibility to this nation as long as he persists in trying to force this parliament to adopt a design which he realizes a large proportion of the members of the house find totally unacceptable.

Mr. Speaker, on a point of order, Your Honour pointed out some time ago to the hon. member that the question to which he should be addressing himself was that of a referendum. I have listened to the

Canadian Flag
hon. member with considerable attention, and I fail to see how the remarks he has made to this time are relevant to the matter now before the house.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to speak to the point of order. I think it would be a good thing to invite the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. Moreau) to occupy the chair for a while.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member who has the floor indicated a moment ago that this is the question to which he intended to address himself. I know he recognizes that, in view of the fact he has already spoken in the debate on the amendment, he is perhaps in a position where he should as much as possible limit his remarks to the specific question before the house. I feel that to some extent he has done that until now, but I would invite him to keep this in mind.

Surely, Mr. Speaker, when I am discussing two of the particular designs that are involved in the subamendment, I must be talking to the question before the house. If I am not, then I do not know when I would be. The point I was trying to make was that we cannot continue forever in this fashion, so long as the government persists with its plan to make parliament accept the design it is proposing at the present time. There are too many members in this house who say this design is totally unacceptable.
Hear, hear.

Surely, Mr. Speaker, in view of this fact, if the Prime Minister is determined to produce a flag he must move in the direction of trying to produce one that is acceptable to a majority, and a large majority. I might refer to the suggestion made by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming), that a flag is not something that should be decided upon by a bare majority of the members of the House of Commons. Surely we should have the type of support in the House of Commons, for whatever new flag is accepted, which will mean that at least two thirds of the members of this house find the design acceptable to them, which would be an indication that at least two thirds of the people of this nation found the design acceptable. At the moment there are 50 per cent of the people of this country either in favour of the design the Prime Minister has produced, or some other design, and 50 per cent of the people-or close to that percentage-are in favour of the present flag. There is no hope of ever reaching a conclusion of a debate

based on two propositions when there is not any strong support for either one.
I might refer for a moment to the speech of the hon. member for York East (Mr. Otto). If he did anything, he made one point abundantly clear. He said he did not imagine there would be the support in the country for the Canadian red ensign that is evident today. I think when this debate started there was not this degree of support for the Canadian red ensign, or else people had not made up their minds about the flag; they had not thought about it. However, Mr. Speaker, the problem is that suddenly they became aware of the fact that there was going to be a change, and they looked at the Canadian red ensign and saw it as a flag that represented freedom and liberty. When they saw what was going on, they rushed to this flag because it had provided in the past this freedom and liberty. What better reason is there, what better example of why we should have a flag that is representative of our past history and tradition, if it is not for the fact that at times of doubt people look to it and see in it those things that are representative of the history, tradition and liberty that we so dearly love.
In concluding my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I would ask the Prime Minister to give leadership to the country in this matter; to admit that what he has produced in this resolution with regard to a flag is not something which at this time the nation is willing to accept; that it is one which does not carry the large majority that is needed in the House of Commons for the adoption of a national flag. This majority is not available to him. The Prime Minister should either withdraw his resolution and introduce another which is more acceptable, or honestly say to the Canadian people, "This is not the time, I have found, to go forward with a new flag design. The Canadian nation is not ready for a new flag. I hate to admit this, but I have honestly found this out, and in all sincerity I now withdraw the flag resolution that I introduced into the House of Commons".
Mr. Speaker, many Canadians would have more respect for our Prime Minister if he were willing to adopt this attitude, rather than the attitude of endeavouring to produce a flag and foist it on the Canadian people, aggravating thousands, if not millions of people who do not want this flag, will not accept it and will not respect it even if it is pushed through this House of Commons. That is the thing that bothers me more than anything else; I do not want to think that we in

the House of Commons are going to adopt a flag that a great many people in this nation will have no respect for, once it is hoisted on the flagpoles of this country.
Mr. Speaker, I see it is six o'clock.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask about the business of the house, particularly the estimates that will be called for Friday.
Business of the House Mr. Favreau: Mr. Speaker, I take it that the flag debate will continue tomorrow. On Friday-if we reach Friday-we will proceed with the examination of the estimates of the Department of Forestry, to be followed by the estimates of the Department of Industry, to be followed by the completion of the discussion on the estimates of the Department of Citizenship and Immigration.
At six o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.
